stumbles.quote: Remex can use 4,096 k-means centroids as index cells.
stumbles.why: "Remex" is never explained (a library? a quantizer?). Its "hash cells" and "1-bit quantization" are also undefined, so the comparison has no clear baseline.

stumbles.quote: Remex's hash cells hold 70% and scan 34% to get there.
stumbles.why: "Get there" is ambiguous. It could mean reaching 90% recall or reaching 70%. If it means 90%, the text contradicts itself, because it says the hash cells hold 70%. Which hash configuration is used is also not stated.

stumbles.quote: Oskar sent the e-means page (arXiv 2611.09501) on 2026-11-10 with a note: "I am certain you can find a way to make use of this and build upon our prior work."
stumbles.why: Oskar and "our prior work" are never explained. e-means is never defined either, and it is not clear how it differs from k-means. The arXiv number 2611 would also imply a November 2026 posting, which is the same day as the email.

stumbles.quote: I assumed e-means would mainly speed up training, so I spent the first hour benchmarking speed.
stumbles.why: The text never says what e-means is. "Passes" and "iterations" are not related to each other, so the speed claim is hard to interpret.

stumbles.quote: e-means matches the error of 25 iterations of Lloyd's k-means in 1 to 3 passes. On 4 CPUs that is 1.6 to 10.2 times sooner.
stumbles.why: The unit of "pass" is undefined. The 1.6–10.2× range is not tied to the 1–3 passes. It is also unclear which k and which dimension were used.

stumbles.quote: Lloyd and e-means centroids give the same recall within 0.005
stumbles.why: Recall is not defined here. It could be index-cell recall, recall@10, or something else. The setup is also unspecified, for example the number of cells probed.
The baseline is not stated. It is probably remex 1-bit without centroid offsets, but the text does not say so. It is also unclear whether this is the same experiment as the 90% cell figure.

stumbles.quote: the centroid table costs 126 bytes per vector, which is more than adding a second bit per dimension would cost.
stumbles.why: Both numbers depend on the dimension, which is not given. A 4,096-centroid table amortised over 100,000 vectors does not obviously come to 126 bytes per vector, so the arithmetic cannot be checked. The cost of a second bit per dimension is not stated.

stumbles.quote: I had expected the offset coding to be the win and the index cells to be a side note. It came out the other way.
stumbles.why: This contradicts the earlier statement that the author expected e-means to speed up training. The text names two different expectations without reconciling them.

point: Using 4,096 k-means centroids as index cells for remex gave much better recall per fraction of corpus scanned than hash cells (90% at 0.56% scanned versus 70% at 34%), while e-means mostly just speeds up training and centroid-offset coding was not worth its storage cost.
